title: Maximum Units on a Truck
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every count combination versus sorting box types by units-per-box and greedily filling truck capacity.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: You have boxTypes, where boxTypes[i] = [numberOfBoxesi, numberOfUnitsPerBoxi]. You must put boxes on a truck with a maximum capacity of truckSize boxes (of any types combined). Return the MAXIMUM total number of units that can be put on the truck.

blocks.text: Since the truck has a fixed capacity in NUMBER OF BOXES (not weight or volume), and every box counts the same toward this capacity regardless of type, the best strategy is to fill the truck with boxes from the type offering the MOST units per box first, then the next best, and so on, until the truck is full or all boxes are loaded.

blocks.title: Analogy: Filling a Limited Number of Shopping Bags with the Most Valuable Items
blocks.text: Picture having room for only a fixed NUMBER of shopping bags (not a weight limit), and wanting to maximize total value, with each type of item worth a different fixed amount per bag. Filling your limited bag slots with the highest-value item type first, then the next best, and so on, clearly maximizes total value.

blocks.caption: Sort box types by units per box descending, then greedily fill truck capacity starting with the best type

blocks.text: Result: 8. Prioritizing the 3-units-per-box type: take 1 box (3 units), then the 2-units-per-box type: take 2 boxes (4 units), reaching truckSize=3 boxes used, wait recompute: sorted by units desc: [1,3],[2,2],[3,1]; take 1 box of 3units=3, take 2 boxes of 2units=4, total 3 boxes used, 1 remaining capacity, take 1 box of 1unit=1; total=3+4+1=8.

Before trying every possible combination of box counts summing to truckSize, notice that since every box occupies exactly ONE unit of truck capacity regardless of type, always preferring the highest units-per-box type available is unambiguously optimal, no trade-off analysis needed beyond sorting.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Truck capacity is measured strictly in NUMBER of boxes, so a box from any type "costs" exactly the same amount of capacity (1 slot).

Observation 2: Given this, filling the truck with as many of the HIGHEST units-per-box type as possible, before moving to the next-best type, can never be beaten by any other allocation, since swapping a lower-value box for a higher-value one (when both cost the same capacity) always helps or ties.

Observation 3: Sorting box types by units-per-box descending, then greedily taking min(available count, remaining truck capacity) from each type in order, directly implements this strategy.

Observation 4: Stopping once truck capacity is exhausted (or all box types have been considered) correctly computes the maximum achievable total units.
This leads to sorting box types by units-per-box descending, then greedily filling truck capacity by taking as many boxes as possible from each type in that order, until the truck is full.
Try every possible combination of box counts (one count per type, each between 0 and its available count) summing to at most truckSize, tracking the maximum total units.

items: Recursively decide, for each box type, how many boxes of it to take (from 0 up to its available count).
Track the running truck capacity used and total units accumulated.
Once all types are decided, if capacity was not exceeded, compare the total units to the best found so far.

codes.python:
def maximum_units_brute(box_types, truck_size):
    n = len(box_types)
    best = [0]

    def helper(i, remaining_capacity, total):
        if i == n or remaining_capacity == 0:
            best[0] = max(best[0], total)
            return
        count, units = box_types[i]
        for take in range(min(count, remaining_capacity) + 1):     # try every possible count
            helper(i + 1, remaining_capacity - take, total + take * units)

    helper(0, truck_size, 0)
    return best[0]

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible count combination directly explores every valid loading, guaranteed correct.
This costs an enormous number of combinations (product of possible counts per type), completely infeasible beyond tiny inputs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential (product of per-type choice counts).
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: since every box costs the same capacity regardless of type, a simple greedy sort-and-fill strategy is provably optimal, achieving O(n log n) instead of exponential exploration.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every combination is unnecessary: because every box occupies exactly one truck slot regardless of its type, the problem reduces to "fill fixed slots with the highest-value items available," a textbook greedy scenario.

The exchange argument: if any allocation uses a lower units-per-box type while a higher units-per-box type still has boxes available and truck capacity was used elsewhere on the lower type, swapping preserves or improves the total, since both boxes cost the same capacity.

The greedy algorithm: sort box types by units-per-box descending; for each type in order, load min(available count, remaining truck capacity) boxes, accumulating their total units, until the truck is full.

The core idea: sort once, then greedily fill in O(n log n) total.

Sort box types by units-per-box descending. For each type in order, take min(count, remaining truck capacity) boxes, adding their units to the total and reducing remaining capacity; stop once capacity reaches 0.

blocks.caption: Sort by units per box descending, then greedily fill remaining truck capacity

blocks.text: Since every box, regardless of type, occupies exactly one unit of truck capacity, maximizing total units is equivalent to filling the fixed capacity with the highest "value per slot" items first. Any allocation that used a lower-value box while a higher-value box was still available and unused elsewhere could be improved by swapping them (both cost the same capacity), so the greedy sort-and-fill strategy is provably optimal.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) if the sort is not in-place).

blocks.text: Maximum Units on a Truck is a clean example of the fractional-knapsack-style greedy: when every item "costs" the same capacity regardless of type, always take the highest-value type first.

items: Sorting by total units (count times unitsPerBox) instead of units PER box, which would incorrectly prioritize types with many low-value boxes over fewer high-value ones.
Forgetting to cap the take amount at the remaining truck capacity, potentially overloading the truck.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "since every box costs the same capacity, this is a fractional-knapsack-style greedy: sort by value per slot, fill greedily" ties this problem to a well-known broader technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "maximize value given a fixed COUNT capacity, where each item costs the same", think: sort by value per item descending, greedily fill.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Trying every count combination costs exponential time; sorting descending and greedily filling costs O(n log n) time, both O(1) extra space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: fractional-knapsack-style greedy, sorting by value per unit of capacity and filling greedily.
Core Idea: sort box types by units per box descending; take as many boxes as possible from each type in order until truck capacity is exhausted.
Time: exponential for trying every combination, O(n log n) for the optimized sort-and-fill.
Space: O(n) recursion depth versus O(1) extra.
Most Important Observation: since every box costs the same truck capacity, always preferring the highest-value type is unambiguously optimal.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible fractional-knapsack-style greedy problem.
One line memory trick: sort by units per box descending, greedily fill remaining capacity.
